planting.note: Root softwood cuttings or set out container specimens after all frost risk has passed; Lohengrin is a long-grown tropical hibiscus cultivar valued for its large, soft pink single flowers with deeper pink throat veining.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Lohengrin produces large, single, soft pink flowers with a rosy blush deepening toward the throat, a gentler pastel counterpart to the bold reds and oranges common among older tropical hibiscus cultivars. The vigorous, well-branched shrub blooms continuously through the warm season and has remained popular with collectors for its clean, classic flower form. Prune hard in late winter or early spring to renew wood and maximize bloom count, and feed with a slow-release fertilizer through the growing season.

common_name: Anderson Crepe Hibiscus (Ruffled Red Tropical Hibiscus)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings or set out container specimens after all frost risk has passed; Anderson Crepe is a classic Gulf South heirloom hibiscus grown for its heavily crinkled, crepe-textured red petals.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Anderson Crepe is an old Southern favorite prized for its large single red flowers with distinctively ruffled, crepe-paper-textured petals, giving the bloom a fuller, more textured appearance than smooth-petaled hibiscus cultivars. The shrub is vigorous and free-flowering, producing a steady succession of blooms from spring through frost in warm climates, and has persisted in Gulf Coast dooryard gardens for generations. Prune hard in late winter to shape and renew growth, and feed regularly through the growing season for best bloom production.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring into cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this New Zealand alpine-woodland perennial dislikes hot, humid summers and performs best where nights stay cool.

directions: Set out divisions or nursery starts in spring in cool, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, in dappled or full shade. Native to montane forest margins and stream banks of New Zealand, mountain foxglove forms a spreading mat of large, softly hairy, scalloped leaves from which tall, wiry stems rise in early summer bearing loose spikes of white, foxglove-like flowers with yellow throats. It struggles in hot, humid summer climates and is best suited to cool, maritime or high-elevation gardens with reliable moisture; mulch to keep roots cool and divide congested clumps in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant creeping divisions in spring in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, choosing a sheltered spot out of drying wind and hot afternoon sun; this Chilean woodland species spreads by creeping stolons and resents summer heat and drought.

directions: Plant creeping divisions in spring in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, choosing a sheltered spot out of drying wind and hot afternoon sun. Native to the temperate rainforests of Chile and Argentina, scarlet ourisia spreads by surface stolons into a low mat of rounded, toothed leaves, sending up short stems topped with brilliant scarlet, tubular flowers in summer that draw hummingbirds in its native range. It needs constant cool moisture and struggles wherever summers are hot or humid, making it best suited to maritime or high-humidity coastal gardens with mild summers; topdress with leaf mold annually and lift and replant vigorous runners to keep the patch tidy.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall into cool, moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; like other Paris species it is slow to establish and resents disturbance once settled.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist woodland soil in partial to full shade. Farges' Paris is a Chinese woodland relative of herb paris, producing a single whorl of broad, net-veined leaves atop each stem, topped in late spring by a curious star-shaped flower with narrow green sepals, thread-like yellow-green petals, and a dark purple-black ovary that persists into an ornamental seed capsule. It spreads slowly by rhizome and takes several years to reach flowering size from division, so choose a permanent, undisturbed site with steady moisture and dappled shade. Established clumps need little attention beyond an annual mulch of leaf litter to mimic its native forest floor.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring, or in fall in mild climates; Crusader is self-fertile so a single bush will set fruit, though yields improve with a second black currant nearby. Like its siblings Consort and Coronet, Crusader carries partial resistance to white pine blister rust, making it a lower-risk choice where Ribes plantings are regulated near white pine stands.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in moist, fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, since black currants are shallow-rooted and dislike drying out. Crusader was bred at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva alongside 'Consort' and 'Coronet' specifically to carry resistance to white pine blister rust, the fungal disease that led many US states to restrict or ban Ribes cultivation for decades. Its parentage from resistant wild currant stock gives it a slightly more assertive, tart flavor than European dessert-type black currants, so fruit is best suited to jams, syrups, cassis, and baking rather than fresh eating. Crusader needs real winter chill and struggles in hot-summer climates; prune out canes older than three years each dormant season to keep the bush productive, since fruit forms mainly on one- and two-year-old wood.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Rust-Resistant Black Currant Cultivars
New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva — Ribes Breeding Program
University of Minnesota Extension — Growing Currants and Gooseberries

planting.note: Nick seed coats and soak overnight, then sow as early as soil can be worked; where winters are mild, an autumn sowing overwinters for earlier bloom.

directions: Introduced in 1938, this striking heirloom carries slate-grey and violet stripes flaking over a smoky white ground, unlike any solid-colored sweet pea of its era. The unusual marbled coloring darkens slightly as blooms age, giving mixed bouquets an antique, storm-cloud cast. Provide netting or brushy pea stakes at sowing since the vigorous vines climb quickly by tendril alone. Cut stems regularly for the vase to keep the plant setting new buds rather than pods through the cool part of the season.
sources: Select Seeds heirloom sweet pea catalog
Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

planting.note: Nick seed coats and soak overnight before direct sowing as soon as the ground can be worked; support with netting at sowing time.

directions: This exhibition-style heirloom bears cream-white standards and wings finely picoteed in rose-lavender along the ruffled edge, giving each bloom a delicate, hand-painted look. The old-fashioned grandiflora form keeps the clove-like scent that many modern picotee types have traded away for larger flowers. Deadhead or pick blooms every two to three days to prevent pod set and keep vines flowering through the cool season. Grow it up a trellis or pea netting in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost before sowing.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

planting.note: Nick seed coats and soak overnight, then direct sow as early as soil can be worked; vines climb readily once given support.

directions: Dating to 1891, this Eckford-era heirloom flakes deep chocolate-maroon over an ivory ground, producing a striped, almost tortoiseshell effect that stands out in a mixed bouquet. Flowers carry the strong, sweet fragrance typical of the earliest grandiflora introductions. Set up a trellis or brushy pea stakes at sowing time, since the older, smaller-flowered types still climb vigorously once established. Harvest stems often to prolong bloom, as this variety, like other Victorian heirlooms, stops flowering quickly once pods are allowed to form.
sources: Select Seeds heirloom sweet pea catalog
Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

common_name: Flora Norton Sweet Pea (Clear Blue Victorian Grandiflora)

planting.note: Nick seed coats and soak overnight, then sow direct as soon as soil can be worked; fall sowing suits mild-winter climates.

directions: Bred by Henry Eckford and introduced in 1904, this heirloom was long considered the clearest true-blue sweet pea of its generation, holding its color without fading to mauve as many older blues do. Compact, ruffle-free grandiflora flowers pack the strong old-fashioned sweet pea scent onto shorter stems than modern Spencer types. Give the vines netting or brush at sowing time so tendrils can climb from the start. Pick regularly through the cool season to delay pod formation and keep the vines productive.
sources: Select Seeds heirloom sweet pea catalog
Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

common_name: Miss Willmott Sweet Pea (Salmon-Orange Victorian Grandiflora)

planting.note: Nick seed coats and soak overnight before direct sowing as early as the ground can be worked; support vines with netting from the start.

directions: Introduced in 1901 and named for the celebrated English horticulturist, this Eckford-raised heirloom opens a warm salmon-orange that was considered a novel break from the pinks, mauves, and blues common at the time. Small, intensely fragrant grandiflora blooms sit on wiry stems well suited to posy-style arrangements. Enrich the bed with compost before sowing, since this older variety flowers best in fertile, evenly moist soil. Cut frequently to prevent pod set and extend bloom through the cool season.
sources: Select Seeds heirloom sweet pea catalog
Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

common_name: Prima Donna Sweet Pea (Original Rose-Pink Spencer)

planting.note: Nick seed coats and soak overnight, then direct sow as early as soil can be worked; provide sturdy netting or a trellis at sowing time for the tall vines.

directions: First introduced around 1911 as one of the earliest true Spencer-type sweet peas, this heirloom bears clear rose-pink, generously waved and ruffled standards over lighter pink wings, a form that set the template for the large, frilled Spencer types grown today. Vigorous vines run taller than older grandiflora varieties and need a sturdy trellis or netting from the start. Pick blooms every few days to keep vines producing rather than setting seed pods. Feed lightly and keep soil evenly moist through the cool growing season for the longest stems.
sources: Select Seeds heirloom sweet pea catalog
Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

common_name: Lady Grisel Hamilton Sweet Pea (Lavender Victorian Grandiflora)

planting.note: Nick seed coats and soak overnight before direct sowing as soon as the ground can be worked; give young vines netting or brush to climb.

directions: Raised by Henry Eckford at the turn of the twentieth century, this heirloom produces soft pale-lavender flowers with a faint blue undertone, a shade prized for the muted, old-fashioned bouquets so distinct from the vivid Spencer hybrids that followed it. Compact grandiflora blooms carry the intense, sweet fragrance characteristic of pre-1900 varieties. Enrich the soil with compost ahead of sowing and keep vines evenly watered for the best flower production. Harvest stems often through the cool season to delay pod set and prolong bloom.
sources: Select Seeds heirloom sweet pea catalog
Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

planting.note: Nick seed coats and soak overnight, then direct sow as early as soil can be worked; set netting or a trellis in place at sowing time.

directions: Bred by New Zealand sweet pea breeder Dr. Keith Hammett, this modern variety pairs pure white, old-fashioned-sized blooms with a fragrance strong enough to rival heirloom grandifloras, a combination that made it a favorite among exhibitors and scent-focused cutting gardeners. The relatively short standards and wings keep the flower shape close to Victorian type despite its recent breeding. Pick blooms every two to three days to prevent pod formation and keep vines flowering. Grow up sturdy netting in fertile soil with consistent moisture through the cool season.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes
